title: Never write another employment verification letter by hand
summary: Learn how to write and send an employment verification letter using an AI assistant.
body_text: Employment verification letters are the kind of task that tends to be urgent but arrives when you’re in the middle of something else. An employee is closing on a mortgage or signing a lease, and they need a letter today. So you stop what you're doing, look for a template, dig through records for their title and start date, and double-check the details, all for a document that says what your payroll and HR system already knows. The good news is that, if you use an AI assistant like Claude or ChatGPT, and it’s connected to your employee directory, you can easily create an employment verification letter in seconds. Ask for the letter in plain language and get back an accurate, ready-to-send draft pulled straight from your employee records. You can even ask the employee’s manager to review the letter, *and* send the approved letter to your employee, all through an AI assistant. Below, we walk step-by-step through how to write and send an employment verification letter using an AI assistant. For Plane users, you can do this through our MCP server or Plane Agent, your AI teammate in Slack, so we’ll use Plane in our walkthrough. Watch it in action Prefer a two-minute version? Learn how to write and send an employment verification letter using an AI assistant in this video from Emily at Plane. Option A: Use your AI assistant with Plane's MCP server If your team already works in an AI assistant like Claude or ChatGPT, you can connect it to Plane once and ask for letters right there. Setting up your MCP connection Before you start, you’ll connect your assistant to Plane. In an MCP-compatible client, add Plane as a remote connector using the link below. For more detailed instructions, check out our MCP guide . Step 1: Ask for the letter Describe what you need the same way you'd explain it to an assistant or any other colleague. Name the employee and the details to include: A quick note on control: you decide what goes in. Leave salary out by saying so, as above, and add a specific recipient, such as a bank or a landlord, if the letter should be addressed to someone in particular. Step 2 (optional): Route it for approval first Plane knows who each employee reports to, so you don't have to look it up. Ask the assistant to find the manager and prepare the approval request: If your assistant is connected to your email or Slack, it can drop the request straight into a draft for your review. Nothing sends until you say so. Step 3: Send it Once the letter is approved, ask the assistant to draft the email to the recipient with the letter attached. You can even come back later and ask "Did the manager reply?" and your assistant reads the response and updates the letter if they asked for a change. Option B: Ask Plane Agent in Slack If you'd rather not leave Slack, Plane Agent brings the same capability into the channels you already use. Setting up Plane Agent To turn on Plane Agent in Slack, sign into your Plane account and go to the Features catalog. Note that Plane Agent is currently in beta. Step 1: Ask for the letter Describe it in plain language, just as above: Step 2 (optional): Route it for approval Ask Plane Agent to send the draft to the right person before it goes out: Plane pulls the reporting relationship from the employee's record and drafts the request for you. You don't have to watch for the reply. Come back later and ask "Did Jordan's manager reply?" and Plane will read their feedback and update the letter for you to confirm. Step 3: Review and send Plane Agent returns a complete draft built from current records, in PDF form. Read it over, ask it to make any edits, and send it to the employee, right from Slack. What you'll need For Plane Agent, you'll need it enabled in your Slack workspace (via the Features catalog). For the MCP route, you'll need an MCP-compatible AI client such as Claude or ChatGPT connected to Plane. To route approvals and send automatically, connect your assistant to Slack or email. Congrats! The letter that used to interrupt your flow becomes a quick task. Plane already has all the info you need and can do the work for you. Want to learn more about how Plane's open API, MCP, and CLI can help you ditch the busywork of payroll, HR & compliance? We're happy to chat with you. Set up a call with our team.

Considere a pressão sobre um engenheiro diagnosticando problemas de equipamentos em campo, um entregador lutando contra condições climáticas extremas, um colaborador de armazém gerenciando um aumento súbito de pedidos, ou um profissional de saúde coordenando o atendimento ao paciente durante um turno caótico. Nestes momentos críticos, a tecnologia em suas mãos funciona como seu elo vital para dados, colegas e sucesso. O dispositivo que ele usa deve funcionar, sem falhas. Muitas organizações enfrentam uma escolha tentadora: equipar suas equipes com dispositivos familiares, de menor preço e voltados para o consumidor ou investir em tecnologia robusta feita sob medida. Embora as economias iniciais de dispositivos de consumo pareçam atraentes, um olhar mais profundo revela uma história diferente. A verdadeira durabilidade vai muito além de um simples teste de queda; abrange todo o ciclo de vida do dispositivo e seu impacto em suas operações. A escolha certa cria uma base para operações inteligentes que pagam dividendos em produtividade e confiabilidade. Os Custos Ocultos do 'Suficiente' Escolher um dispositivo móvel com base em seu preço inicial muitas vezes ignora o custo total de propriedade (TCO). Um dispositivo de consumo pode sobreviver a uma queda em um teste controlado, mas será que resiste a milhares de vibrações repetidas em um caminhão de entregas, suporta poeira em um armazém movimentado ou aguenta os protocolos constantes de limpeza em um hospital? O relatório IDC MarketScape sobre dispositivos robustos aponta uma realidade crucial: dispositivos robustos de nível empresarial, embora com um custo inicial mais alto, frequentemente resultam em um TCO menor. Dispositivos de consumo geralmente têm ciclos de vida mais curtos, taxas de falha mais altas em ambientes exigentes e exigem substituições mais frequentes. Cada falha vai além da conta de reparo, incluindo tempo de inatividade potencial, perda de produtividade e um trabalhador de linha de frente frustrado, incapaz de realizar seu trabalho. Ao calcular esses custos "imateriais", a proposta de valor de um dispositivo verdadeiramente robusto se torna cristalina. Deixa de ser uma despesa e se mostra como um investimento estratégico na continuidade operacional. Design orientado para a finalidade para uma Linha de frente conectada Os profissionais da linha de frente precisam de ferramentas projetadas para seus fluxos de trabalho específicos. Um dispositivo de consumo, criado para uso casual, não possui os recursos especializados que otimizam a eficiência em ambientes corporativos. É aqui que o design orientado para a finalidade faz a diferença tangível. Recursos como baterias de alta capacidade e trocáveis a quente garantem que um dispositivo dure por um turno inteiro, eliminando a necessidade de parar para recarregar. Telas legíveis à luz do sol permitem que os funcionários de serviços de campo vejam informações críticas sob luz solar intensa, e scanners de código de barras dedicados capturam dados muito mais rápido e com maior precisão do que a câmera de um smartphone. Esses recursos capacitam uma linha de frente conectada de verdade. Eles fornecem insights em tempo real e promovem a colaboração conectada entre os membros da equipe. Quando o hardware funciona em harmonia com as tarefas do usuário, ele simplifica os fluxos de trabalho e permite que os funcionários se concentrem no que mais importa: atender os clientes, movimentar mercadorias e cuidar dos pacientes. Essa engenharia cuidadosa, fruto de décadas de liderança de mercado em soluções de captura de dados, ajuda a melhorar o trabalho todos os dias para suas equipes e para as pessoas que elas atendem. Um ecossistema de inteligência e suporte O hardware em si é apenas parte da equação. Uma solução verdadeiramente robusta com tecnologia AI também inclui um ecossistema abrangente de softwares e serviços que protegem, gerenciam e otimizam o dispositivo durante toda a sua vida útil. title: Warm interior design is back, and it helps homes sell
summary: Warm interiors are back. Five simple rules for colors, walls, floors and lighting that make a listing feel welcoming and help it sell faster.
body_text: Did you know warm interiors are making a comeback? After years of grey floors and cold white walls, people want homes that feel calm and comfortable. That matters when you are selling. A warm room stops looking like a property and starts feeling like home. Here is how to get that look. The basics 5 simple rules 1: Choose warm colors. Cream instead of white. Beige instead of grey. Honey wood instead of grey wood. 2: Never mix warm and cold. A warm wood floor with a cold grey sofa looks wrong, even if you cannot say why. Pick one side and stay there. 3: Add three textures. A rug, a knit throw, linen curtains. Smooth, flat rooms look like showrooms. 4: Turn on the lamps. Soft yellow bulbs, placed low in the room. Two lamps always beat one bright ceiling light. 5: Add round shapes. An oval table, a round rug, a curved chair. Rooms made only of squares feel like an office. Walls Walls fill most of every photo, so start here. Safest: warm white or off white. Cozier: warm beige. For character: soft clay or dusty pink. Skip: cool grey and bright builder white. Finish: matte, not shiny. Shiny paint looks cold. Floors Best: medium warm wood, like oak or honey tones. Hard to work with: grey wood, cold white tile, shiny dark laminate. The fix: one big warm rug in jute, wool or rust. It covers a cold floor instantly. Rug size: the front legs of every sofa and chair should sit on it. What to add in each room Living room: oat or camel sofa, wood coffee table, big soft rug, two lamps, a throw and cushions. Bedroom: cream linen bedding, a throw at the foot, wood nightstands, a small lamp on each side. Kitchen: a wooden board, a bowl of fruit, a linen towel, one plant. Clear the rest of the counter. Dining room: wood table, a ceramic centerpiece, and a warm light hanging low above it. Entryway: console table, mirror, small lamp, plant. Often the first photo buyers see. Why warm rooms sell faster Warm rooms stand out in a long list of thumbnails, they quietly cover dated finishes and small spaces, and they let buyers picture their life in the home instead of judging it. That is what turns a viewing into an offer. The easy way The shortcut All of this is easy until you have to rent real furniture and shoot the room again. Apply Design has ready warm interior design bundles you can simply pick and apply to your photo. And if you like doing it yourself, there are dozens of furniture pieces to play around with. FAQ Questions people ask What is AI interior design? Software that redesigns a room from a photo. You upload the picture, pick a style, and it gives you back the same room with new colors, furniture and lighting. Can AI make a room look warm? Yes. Warm design is mostly color and light, which is exactly what these tools change well. Pick a warm style and the walls, floors, wood tones and lamps all move together. What is virtual staging? Adding furniture and decor to a photo of an empty room instead of renting real furniture. It is the fastest way to show a buyer what a space could look like. Is AI home staging allowed in a listing? In most markets yes, as long as you say the photos are virtually staged. Check your local MLS rules before you publish. How long does AI staging take? Minutes for a room, against days for physical staging, and there is no furniture to move. A color palette to help you Build a room from these and it is hard to go wrong. Cream Walls, bedding Oat Sofas, rugs Sand Walls, curtains Camel Leather, throws Terracotta Cushions, vases Olive Chairs, plants Chocolate Wood, frames Use these Oak Walnut Rattan Linen Wool Jute Tan leather Ceramic Brass Skip these Bright white Cool grey Mint Icy blue Chrome Glass and steel Shiny surfaces

body_text: Sustained Growth Momentum, with Revenues Growing 26.1% YoY and NOI increasing 27.0% SAN JOSÉ, Costa Rica, August 12, 2026 -Logistic Properties of the Americas (NYSE American: LPA) (together with its subsidiaries, “LPA” or “the Company”) announced today its unaudited consolidated financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026 (“second quarter 2026” or “2Q26”). The financial results are expressed in U.S. dollars and are presented in accordance with International Accounting Standard (“IAS”) 34 – Interim Financial Reporting, as issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (“IASB”), which differs in certain significant respects from the U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (“GAAP”). This information should be read in conjunction with, and is qualified in its entirety by reference to, the Company’s condensed consolidated interim financial statements, including the notes thereto. All comparisons within this announcement are year-over-year (“YoY”), unless otherwise noted. LPA’s financial results are stated in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. LPA is a leading developer, owner, acquirer and manager of logistics and industrial real estate of institutional quality in the Americas, and one of the few internally managed, vertically integrated, and institutional-quality platforms operating across the region. 2Q26 Financial and Operating Highlights Total revenue increased 26.1% to $14.7 million in 2Q26. Growth was led by a 50.4% increase in rental revenue in Peru, primarily reflecting PepsiCo’s lease at Callao Logistics Park and the rapid lease-up of space that was scheduled to be vacated. Rental revenue increased 29.3% in Colombia, driven by new leasing, contractual local inflation adjustments and favorable foreign exchange movements; without the foreign exchange accounting effect, the increase in Colombia’s revenue would have been 11.0%. In addition, Mexico contributed $0.5 million of revenue from the two investment properties acquired in Puebla in August 2025. Net Operating Income (“NOI”) increased 27.0% to $12.2 million in 2Q26, driven by higher rental revenue across the Peru and Colombia segments and by Mexico’s revenue contribution, which began in 3Q25. Same-Property Cash NOI increased 15.6% to $9.9 million in 2Q26 on a constant-currency basis, primarily due to higher rental rates and increased occupancy. Operating GLA increased 9.7% to 5.8 million square feet across 34 operating properties, compared to 5.3 million square feet across 31 operating properties as of June 30, 2025. Average rent per square foot increased 10.0% to $8.88, primarily driven by contractual rent escalators, positive leasing spreads, and the favorable currency effect in Colombia. As of June 30, 2026, the occupancy rate in LPA’s operating portfolio was 100.0%, compared to 94.5% as of June 30, 2025. General and administrative expenses decreased 8.7% to $4.2 million in 2Q26, primarily reflecting lower corporate reporting and legal expenses. CEO Commentary We delivered yet another exceptional quarter in 2026. Total revenue increased 26.1% year-over-year and NOI expanded 27.0% to a record $12.2 million, extending the earnings momentum of our unique regional logistics platform. Peru again led growth as PepsiCo’s LEED Gold-certified facility at our Callao park contributed a full quarter of revenue and as new leases with Inkafarma and other tenants increased revenue from recently delivered space. Colombia also posted strong gains, supported by the lease of U.S.-based retailer PriceSmart, contractual inflation adjustments, and the appreciation of the country’s currency, while our properties in Puebla, Mexico contributed $0.5 million of rental revenue. No less important, the strength of LPA’s underlying portfolio performance was equally impressive. Same-Property Cash NOI increased 15.6% on a constant-currency basis, average rent per square foot rose 10.0%, and stabilized occupancy was 100.0% for a third consecutive quarter. These results showcase the quality of our Class A logistics assets, the depth and durability of demand from global and regional tenants, and the pricing power we command with modern, well-located facilities in markets that remain structurally underserved. They also demonstrate the growing scale advantages of our platform, as G&A expenses declined while operating GLA, revenue and NOI all increased. Another highlight is that our strong performance was broad-based. Peru’s rental revenue grew 50.4% as recently delivered capacity ramped up; Colombia’s rental revenue increased 29.3% through a combination of organic leasing and contractual escalations, and Costa Rica delivered 5.6% growth through renewals and re-leasing at higher rates. Mexico, albeit a still relatively small but soon to be growing portion of our property portfolio, continued to perform in line with our underwriting and added another source of diversified earnings. Across our markets, resilient domestic consumption, accelerating e-commerce adoption, supply chain regionalization, and the chronic structural undersupply of institutional-quality logistics infrastructure continue to support mid- and long-term tenant demand. To effectively capitalize on the various long-term market opportunities before us, we remain focused on disciplined capital allocation, proactive asset management, and long-term value creation as a fully integrated, internally managed logistics and industrial real estate company. With the goal of establishing an additional value lever, we announced during the quarter our strategic alliance with FIBRA Prime, which begins with the pending $145.0 million divestment of Parque Logístico Lima Sur. Subject to customary approvals and closing conditions, the transaction is expected to generate approximately $85.0 million in net proceeds after debt repayment and before taxes, significantly increasing our flexibility to fund LPA’s next phase of growth, primarily in Mexico, and to drive higher returns on capital. In closing, our operating portfolio is fully occupied, while approximately 92% of our 440,383-square-foot development pipeline is pre-leased, including the fourth building at Callao that is fully committed to a regional packaging manufacturer. That contracted backlog gives us visibility into future rental revenue growth and further strengthens LPA’s role as a partner of choice to industry leaders expanding across Latin America’s markets. Quarter after quarter, we are delivering on our vision: bridging local insight with global impact. title: Three REMAX Leaders Recognized as ‘Women of Influence’ Share Their Advice for Success
summary: Following recognition on HousingWire’s 2026 Women of Influence list, the brokerage leaders reflect on growth, resilience and building lasting influence.
body_text: HousingWire named three leaders from the REMAX® network to the 2026 Women of Influence list, an award honoring women whose leadership, innovation and impact are helping shape the future of the housing industry. This year's honorees include Debra Beagle, Managing Broker/Co-Owner and CEO of The Ashton Real Estate Group of REMAX Advantage in Nashville, Tennessee; Stephenie Flood, COO & Vice President of Operations of Gold Nation and REMAX Gold in Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada and Oregon; and Rebecca Zimmerman, VP of Operations of REMAX Advantage – Team Zimmerman in Port Orange, Florida. While each followed a different path to success, common themes emerged when we asked them about the decisions that shaped their careers, the habits successful leaders share and what this recognition means to them. Debra Beagle Stephenie Flood Rebecca Zimmerman Q: Looking back on your career, what was one decision, habit or mindset shift that made the biggest difference in your success? Debra Beagle: "It is hard to settle on just one thing, as I truly see it as a combination of pivots and changes over time. One big shift came when I started treating the business like the analytical discipline it is, reviewing metrics consistently and understanding how decisions affected our agents and staff. More recently, I stopped measuring success by how much we sold and started measuring it by whether the business was actually healthy. Once I made that shift, everything got stronger, including retention, culture and profitability." Stephenie Flood: "I think what's made the biggest difference is saying yes before I felt ready. I started with REMAX Gold in 1997 as a receptionist, and every step from there happened because I raised my hand for opportunities I hadn't done before and trusted I'd figure them out. The front desk turned out to be the best training ground because I learned every piece of how a brokerage actually runs. I've never looked back and still can't remember a time I said no to an opportunity." Rebecca Zimmerman: "For me, it was the shift from doing everything myself to building a team and systems that allowed us to scale. Once we invested in processes, documentation and the right people to own them, we were able to grow in a way that individual effort never could. Bringing in a business coach was also a big part of that shift. I think a lot of agents try to figure it all out alone, and that's usually the slowest path to growth." Q: What's one piece of advice you'd give agents who want to grow their business and influence in today's market? Debra Beagle: "Build systems before you build a bigger book of business. Success and influence follow consistency, not hustle. Agents who scale and sustain are the ones who've documented their processes, leaned into a CRM that actually works for them and built support around them so they can lead instead of just produce." Stephenie Flood: "Stop waiting for things to get easier, because they won't. I've been through the Great Recession and the current downturn, and the pattern is always the same. The agents who succeed aren't the ones waiting for rates to drop or inventory to improve. They're the ones who adapt and grow while others seem frozen. Learn to handle hard better." Rebecca Zimmerman: "Stop trying to do more and start trying to do the right things more consistently. The agents who grow fastest are the ones who've identified the few high-leverage activities that move the needle and show up ready to address those activities every single day. And don't try to do it alone – find a coach or mentor. Someone else may already have the blueprint." Q: What's one thing successful agents and leaders do consistently that others often overlook? Debra Beagle: "They follow up relentlessly, long after most people would've given up. Everyone loves closings; almost nobody loves the repetitive work of staying in touch, checking in and showing up for people who aren't ready yet. The agents who win the most business over time are the ones who never let a relationship go cold." Stephenie Flood: "It's a combination of staying the course and changing. Successful leaders know when to stick with the activities that work over time – marketing outreach, phone calls, the long game – and when to recognize something is no longer producing results and have the courage to try something new." Rebecca Zimmerman: "They know their numbers. Most agents operate on gut feeling and hope, but top performers treat their business like a business. Knowing your numbers gives you a clear path forward. You know exactly what to fix, where to invest and what to do next instead of guessing." Q: HousingWire's Women of Influence recognition celebrates leadership and industry impact. What does this recognition mean to you, and what do you hope other women in real estate take away from it? Debra Beagle: "It's meaningful because it's a reminder that there's a seat at the table for women leading at every level of our industry – not just producing. I hope other women take permission to lead loudly: run for boards, build brands, and take a seat in rooms where real estate policy and strategy get decided. Keep building, keep leading and keep making room for others to rise with you." Stephenie Flood: "It means a great deal because of where I started. Nearly 30 years ago, I was sitting at the front desk. The important thing I want other women to know is that there isn't just one way into leadership. You don't need a perfect résumé or a specific background. Be brave, learn everything you can, take on the work nobody else wants and find people who will champion you. The front desk can lead to the corner office. Mine did." Rebecca Zimmerman: "This recognition means a lot because it reflects not just individual success, but the impact of building something bigger than myself – an amazing team, culture and systems that help other agents thrive. If there's one thing I hope other women take away, it's that leadership doesn't require waiting for permission or a perfect résumé. It comes from stepping up, building the thing you wish existed and bringing others along with you." — Different careers. Different journeys. One shared message: meaningful success comes from continuously learning, adapting and investing in others. It's a lesson that has shaped these leaders' careers and one that can help any agent build lasting influence of their own. body_text: Bakkt Reports Second Quarter 2026 Results August 10, 2026 PDF Version - GAAP net income of $80.8 million, or $1.96 per basic and $1.94 per diluted share - Six commercial offerings live across Bakkt Markets; Total Transacting Volume (“TTV”) of $168.8 million in Q2, including payments volume generated on acquired infrastructure, bringing first-half TTV to $410.0 million - Bakkt Agent Embedded Finance available for partner integration today; initial co-branded card programs and Neobank-as-a-Service offerings targeted for Q4 2026 - Cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash of $50.7 million as of June 30, 2026, with no long-term debt - Received Indian regulatory approvals and completed the allotment of 47.5 million Transchem warrants in June; position carried at a fair value of $107.9 million as of June 30, 2026 ATLANTA, Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Bakkt, Inc. ("Bakkt," "Company," "we" or "us") (NYSE: BKKT) announced its financial and operational results for the quarter and six months ended June 30, 2026 and provided an update on certain business developments. Management Commentary: "Bakkt is building a financial operating system for the AI and token economy through three complementary engines: Bakkt Markets, our regulated infrastructure layer; Bakkt Agent, our intelligence layer; and Bakkt Global, our opportunity layer. During the quarter, we made tangible progress across all three," said Akshay Naheta, CEO of Bakkt. “In Bakkt Markets, we processed approximately $410 million in Total Transacting Volume during the first half, which included payments volume for the first time through infrastructure acquired in April and now operated within Bakkt’s payments stack. Our six live commercial offerings span trading infrastructure, stablecoin and digital-asset OTC, stablecoin on- and off-ramps, cross-border payments and the Bakkt Widget, connected through a common integration framework. Bakkt Agent progressed from architecture to commercial availability for partner integration. Our Embedded Finance platform, including accounts, payments and international transfers, is available to partners today. We are targeting the fourth quarter of 2026 for initial co-branded card programs and Neobank-as-a-Service offerings, subject to applicable product, partner and regulatory requirements. Bakkt Global also reached an important milestone. Following the receipt of the required regulatory approvals in India, Transchem allotted 47.5 million warrants to Bakkt. Beginning May 1, 2026, payments activity processed through the acquired infrastructure is included in Total Transacting Volume. Commercial Organization: The Company strengthened its go-to-market capability during the quarter under Chief Commercial Officer Daniel Ishag, who now leads a unified Commercial department with an expanded and strengthened sales team. The team is actively bringing the platform’s available products to market, including digital asset trading and OTC execution, stablecoin on- and off-ramps, cross-border payments through the Zaira API, the Bakkt Widget, and Bakkt Agent Embedded Finance modules. title: Amazon Bedrock launches Web Search for OpenAI GPT models
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with Amazon Bedrock launches Web Search for OpenAI GPT models
body_text: Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Search on Amazon Bedrock, a built-in server side tool that performs web search entirely within AWS, enabling OpenAI models (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna) to ground responses with current web knowledge while maintaining data residency within your secured AWS environment with zero data egress. Previously, adding web grounding required onboarding a third-party search provider, managing separate API keys and billing, building custom orchestration, and conducting additional compliance reviews for each external vendor. Web Search removes this heavy lifting by enable grounding with a single parameter in an existing API call, with no vendor onboarding, no external APIs to orchestrate, and no additional vendor security reviews to conduct. Web Search is built by Amazon, informed by years of experience across Alexa+, Amazon Quick and Kiro. It combines a web index operated by Amazon, spanning tens of billions of documents refreshed continually, with a built-in knowledge graph that provides verified facts. Rather than returning raw pages, Web Search performs semantic snippet extraction, delivering context-efficient results optimized for the model's context window with low latency. Web Search integrates through a standardized tool-use interface, compatible with the OpenAI Responses API. Simply add the web search tool to your API call, and Bedrock handles the entire search lifecycle server-side; a single API call returns a grounded response with citations. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock is generally available today in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). To get started, read our blog post Introducing Web Search on Amazon Bedrock for foundation model grounding , review the Web Search section in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide for technical documentation, and visit the Amazon Bedrock pricing page for cost details.

title: Actual results MEP estimators are getting with AI-assisted takeoff
summary: New data from more than 4,000 contractors shows how AI-assisted takeoff reduces manual estimating work, increases bid capacity and keeps estimators focused on higher-value decisions.
body_text: By Brooke Stewart, Director of Product Management, Trimble How much can estimators in the MEP (mechanical, electrical and plumbing) sector really gain when Artificial Intelligence (AI) takes on their tedious takeoff tasks? Actual results from thousands of contractors using Trimble applications this year tell a compelling story. AI is essentially acting like additional employees that are easy to work with and hard to compete with when it comes to completing repetitive and previously manual tasks with speed and accuracy. AI capabilities let these contractors add to their bid volume without adding headcount. They also free up actual estimators to spend more time on higher-value, strategic work. MEP leaders know those are essential ingredients for winning more jobs and winning the right jobs at the right margins. This is a summary of results from more than 4,000 contractors in the U.S. using the AI automation capabilities of Trimble MEP estimating applications in the first half of 2026. Results across a smaller sample size in the UK were almost identical. Pre-takeoff: Six hours per user per month The estimators used AI to set an average of 300,000 drawing scales per month automatically, with 97% requiring no manual changes. Eliminating the 15 seconds it would have taken to detect and set each of those scales manually saved a total of 1,213 hours, or two hours per user, each month. Similarly, setting the name across an entire set of plans automatically instead of manually cut 25 seconds per drawing or a total of four hours per user per month. Object counting: 62% Counting an object on a drawing manually takes, on average, three seconds. The estimators counted an average of 460,000 objects each month. That would have been a total of 23,000 minutes for manual counting. In contrast, Trimble AI capabilities automatically counted the objects in 13,800minutes, a time savings of 60%. Estimate comparison: 83% The estimators did an average of one estimate comparison per week. The traditional method of exporting to Excel, manually comparing and documenting changes takes 60 minutes. The AI assistant in the Trimble application cuts the time by 83% to 10 minutes, providing a comprehensive summary of changes written as though it was passed through the lens of an experienced estimator. Estimating is in large part about calculations, but material, equipment labor and other cost aspects are only part of the equation. Contractors can gain a competitive advantage when they also calculate their estimating time and resources. Manually setting drawing scales and names across plan sets, counting objects and measuring lengths are not complicated tasks but they take a lot of time. Contractors can’t hand them off to inexperienced estimators, because accuracy is so critical. Small mistakes lead to lost bids due to overpricing or lost margins due to underbidding. That can leave the best and most experienced estimators spending a disproportionate amount of their time counting objects and tracing lines. Every hour doing this is an hour they can’t spend on analytical and strategic efforts. AI-assisted takeoff capabilities are emerging as a proven strategy for addressing this fundamental estimating challenge. They’re essentially acting as hyper-productive additions to the estimating staff, allowing contractors to turn out more bids without adding headcount or risking accuracy-related mistakes. Finally, for contractors using the AI capabilities of Trimble estimating applications , it’s important to note that AI does not complete or finalize any part of the process. Initial counting and classifying of symbols goes to an estimator for review. The AI highlights each detected symbol directly on the drawing, organized by category, so the estimator can work through one category at a time and quickly spot-check against what is actually there. Each count also carries a confidence rating, so the estimator knows exactly where to focus first—reviewing the lowest-confidence detections before moving on. Nothing gets into a bid without a qualified person putting eyes on it.

title: Moving from Manual Inspection to Machine Vision: A Regulatory Field Guide for Medical Device Quality Teams
summary: Automated visual inspection validation under QMSR: an inspection method change is a letter to file, not a 510(k). Here is the evidence package.
body_text: Grant Nelson Published Aug 14, 2026 • 8 min read Not legal advice. This is general educational information, not regulatory or legal advice. On February 2, 2026, the FDA's Quality System Regulation (QSR) was replaced by the Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR), which incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference (89 FR 7496, published February 2, 2024). This change brings two core updates to computer vision and quality teams at medical device manufacturers : The inspection method changed. The Quality System Inspection Technique (QSIT) has been retired in favor of a QMSR-aligned approach. Internal inspection records are more visible to the FDA. This is the major landmine for teams - a class of internal documents are now subject to FDA review, causing teams to re-evaluate whether their inspection systems are in need of an upgrade. The legacy 820.180(c) exemption that kept management-review minutes, internal audit reports, and supplier audit reports out of routine FDA review has been removed. Under QMSR, FDA can now inspect those records (via 820.35). Many teams have underestimated this: records once written for internal eyes only are now fair game at inspection. In light of this, and advances in the vision AI industry, many teams are thinking about replacing a manual visual inspection step with an automated, camera-based machine vision one. Adopting Automated Computer Vision Inspection Doesn't Change Documentation Requirements Much A Class II device manufacturer (think fusion pumps, motorized wheelchairs, contact lenses ) swapping manual inspection for automated vision inspection will usually handle the change as a retained, inspection-ready "Letter to File", not a new 510(k) submission, as long as the change touches only the manufacturing/ QA process and not the device's design, materials, intended use, or indications for use. That distinction comes from 21 CFR 807.81(a)(3) and the FDA's October 2017 guidance on "Deciding When to Submit a 510(k) for a Change to an Existing Device." If the finished device is unchanged and only how you inspect it is different, the burden shifts from submitting to the agency to documenting for the record . In other words: nothing is filed with FDA in advance. You make the change, you document it thoroughly, and you retain that documentation. FDA may review it reactively , during a routine establishment inspection. That's the good news. The policy goal and the requirements are aligned to encourage companies to improve their inspection coverage and quality by migrating from slow, error-prone manual inspection to highly intelligent automated scaled inspections. 510(k) Letter to File Requirements for Inspection Method Changes The 2017 guidance supersedes the 1997 K97-1 guidance. It walks companies through six decision flowcharts and more than 32 examples. The main question is whether you made the change to significantly improve safety or effectiveness . If not, the flowcharts ask whether residual risks or new failure modes force a submission to the FDA. For an inspection-method change alone, the usual conclusion is that no new 510(k) submission is required. You must demonstrate three things: Nothing changes in the device design, materials, chemical composition, energy source, indications, or intended use. Upgrading to use computer vision for inspection does not trigger a flag here. The new method detects defects at least as well as the method it replaces, supported by method-comparison data. No new failure modes are introduced that can let defective product reach patients. Unless the inspection coverage somehow decreases by adding computer vision, this is usually easily satisfied. Your Letter to File records the change description, the rationale, the risk assessment, the safety-and-effectiveness conclusion, and the supporting validation evidence. Explicitly work through the flowcharts published by the FDA. Two scope notes to keep in mind. The FDA's companion guidance, "Deciding When to Submit a 510(k) for a Software Change to an Existing Device," governs the medical device software, not production software. A vision-inspection retrofit generally does not trigger it. Class III devices (for example pacemakers ) live under a much stricter rule: 21 CFR 814.39 requires a PMA supplement for changes affecting safety or effectiveness, and 814.39(d)(2)(iv) names new manufacturing controls and test methods specifically. Establish A Baseline Your Letter to File will claim the new method performs at least as well as the old one. You cannot prove that claim without a documented picture of the old one. Capture this early: Current SOPs, work instructions, inspection aids, and written acceptance criteria. Historical inspection data: defect rates by category, first-pass yield, sampling records, trend charts. Process capability studies for the manual method. Any gauge R&R and operator qualification studies for manual gauges. Training records for the current inspectors (820.25). Historical CAPAs (Corrective and Preventive Action), deviations, and complaints tied to inspection escapes. Your company should have this data already. If not, implementing a process, perhaps using computer vision immediately to evaluate the baseline is imperative. Required Documentation for Method Changes Think of the change as producing one evidence package. It has a handful of pillars. 1. Validate the process (the IQ/OQ/PQ backbone) Process validation is triggered whenever "the results of a process cannot be fully verified by subsequent inspection and test" (21 CFR 820.75). A vision inspection that outputs a pass/fail or a measurement you can't practically re-check unit-by-unit with a second independent method is the textbook example. The FDA's own process-validation training has long used automated camera inspection as the example. The accepted framework is IQ/OQ/PQ, drawn from GHTF/SG3/N99-10:2004 (Edition 2): Installation Qualification (IQ): objective evidence the system is installed to spec: cameras , lenses, lighting, sensors, controllers, firmware, and network, with utilities verified, calibrations current, and configuration documented. Operational Qualification (OQ): characterizing the operating envelope: lighting and contrast thresholds, defect sensitivity and specificity across worst-case conditions, repeatability, and a confusion matrix against known-defect samples. Performance Qualification (PQ): proving consistent performance on real production units , across operators, shifts, and lots, against pre-defined acceptance criteria. In practice, proving that the computer vision system works on the line in real production shifts satisfies the full ladder. Proving that the system works by running it and comparing its assessment against the human operators (or the previous system) is the point. 2. Validate the implementation A vision inspection system is production/quality-system software, not software as a medical device, so it's governed by 21 CFR 820.70(i). The "Computer Software Assurance (CSA) for Production and Quality System Software" guidance is the key authority. The CSA approach is deliberately risk-based and least-burdensome: you classify each software feature as "high process risk" (a failure could foreseeably compromise safety) or not, and scale your assurance effort accordingly. CSA explicitly endorses unscripted and ad hoc testing for lower-risk features, and lets you leverage vendor-supplied evidence and ISO 13485 supplier certifications rather than re-deriving everything yourself. For a vision system, the final accept/reject decision itself is almost certainly "high process risk" so plan on scripted testing, boundary testing against a curated defect library, and rigorous records of intended use, risk classification, issues and resolutions, tester identity, and dates. Your computer vision system should be able to automatically log samples of defect/no defect for easy review and model retraining. Roboflow customers use our Vision Events product , which logs relevant images from cameras and inspection streams to store and review these examples. 3. Document the statistical rationale This one is frequently under-documented and frequently cited. 21 CFR 820.250 is short but firm: sampling plans, when used, "shall be written and based on a valid statistical rationale," and procedures must be reviewed when changes occur. An inspection-method change is exactly such a trigger. Two paths: If vision enables 100% inspection, document the migration away from sample-based acceptance. If you keep sampling, document the new plan with attributes and variables with a written rationale. Either way, the validation evidence should include the right statistics for the output type: Cpk/Ppk for variable (measurement) outputs. Gauge R&R for measurement systems. Attribute agreement analysis or sensitivity/specificity/ROC analysis for pass/fail classification outputs. The keystone is an equivalence (method-comparison) study on paired samples, ideally including seeded, known defects, showing the new method is at least as capable as the old one. That study is what ultimately backs the Letter-to-File conclusion that safety and effectiveness are not adversely affected. For companies migrating to an automated inspection system, the main driver is often both increased output and safety. So they choose to increase their coverage to 100% of samples, which has the benefit of eliminating statistical sample size as a landmine to trip on. 4. Log the 820.80 Required Records Every acceptance activity must produce a record, and that record goes in the device history record. 21 CFR 820.80(e) lists the required content: Element Citation The acceptance activities performed 820.80(e)(1) Dates of those activities 820.80(e)(2) Results 820.80(e)(3) Signature of the individual conducting the activity 820.80(e)(4) Equipment used, where appropriate 820.80(e)(5) Decide early how to map the inspection system's outputs and image logs to these elements: how acceptances are logged, stored, and retrieved. An automated inspection system should make it easy to generate and access and store the inspection records such as detections, images, and conclusions. 5. Update the risk file and handle rejects ISO 14971:2019 requires you to update the device Risk Management File for the new production control. Record the control itself, its residual risk contribution, and the overall residual risk of the device. The 2019 edition treats production information as an active input to risk review. A vision system will likely be more accurate, resulting in more true positives (rejects) while also reducing false positives (increasing throughput). 21 CFR 820.90 requires procedures for identifying, documenting, evaluating, segregating, and dispositioning nonconforming product. This shouldn't be a new process. 6. Run it through change control 21 CFR 820.70(b) requires procedures for changes to a specification, method, process, or procedure, and mandates that such changes be verified or validated before implementation (per 820.75), with documented activities and 820.40 approval. 21 CFR 820.40 (document controls) requires review, approval, controlled distribution, prompt removal of obsolete documents, and change records capturing the description, affected documents, approver signature, approval date, and effective date. 7. Don't forget people and suppliers Training records (21 CFR 820.25) must cover operators, maintenance technicians, engineers, and quality staff with effectiveness verified. Supplier qualification (21 CFR 820.50) must be current for the vision-system vendor. Where Teams Actually Get Cited The FDA Form 483 observations and warning letters in this exact area are remarkably consistent, and all of them are preventable with the package above: Inadequate process validation: equipment run for years unvalidated, or validation that only checks whether it powers on rather than whether it reliably rejects out-of-spec product. Inadequate software validation: the memorable failure mode being a vision system that accepts out-of-spec product while the investigator watches. Change-control failures: missing verification/validation before implementation, missing approvals, uncontrolled distribution of superseded SOPs. Absent statistical rationale: no documented justification for sample sizes or sampling plans. Further reading on how to make CFR Part 11 compliant solutions with Roboflow: Medical Device Assembly Verification with Vision AI Visual Quality Management System: Automate Defect Detection Automated Visual Inspection for Pharmaceuticals References and Primary Sources Regulations 21 CFR Part 820 (QMSR) 21 CFR 807.81 (510(k) change trigger) 21 CFR 820.75 (process validation) 21 CFR 820.80 (acceptance activities) 21 CFR 820.250 (statistical techniques) Rulemaking QMSR Final Rule, 89 FR 7496 (February 2, 2024) QMSR Technical Amendments (December 4, 2025) FDA guidance "Deciding When to Submit a 510(k) for a Change to an Existing Device" (October 25, 2017) "Computer Software Assurance for Production and Quality System Software" (final September 24, 2025) "General Principles of Software Validation" (January 11, 2002)" QMSR FAQ FDA Inspection Observations data Standards ISO 13485:2016 ISO 14971:2019 GHTF/SG3/N99-10:2004 Ed. 2 (process validation, the IQ/OQ/PQ source) AAMI TIR102:2019 (21 CFR to ISO 13485 mapping, useful as a gap-analysis tool) Cite this Post Use the following entry to cite this post in your research: Grant Nelson . title: How to Plan an Engagement Party
summary: An engagement party is one of the first moments you get to celebrate with the people who matter most, and planning one does not have to be stressful.
body_text: Last Updated on August 14, 2026 by Joy Editors An engagement party is one of the first moments you get to celebrate with the people who matter most, and planning one does not have to be stressful. Whether you are hosting it yourself, a parent is throwing it for you, or a close friend volunteered to take the lead, this guide walks you through every decision from budget and guest list to day-of logistics and decor. Below you will find an eight-week planning checklist, real cost breakdowns by party format, etiquette rules that prevent awkward situations, and invitation wording samples you can copy and customize. We have organized everything so you can skim, bookmark, and return to each section as the party comes together. Quick answer: To plan an engagement party, start by choosing a host and setting a budget. Schedule the event two to four months after the proposal, invite 25 to 50 of your closest friends and family (all of whom must also be invited to the wedding), and send invitations four to six weeks in advance. Most engagement parties last two to four hours and cost between $1,000 and $5,000, depending on venue and guest count. What Is an Engagement Party? An engagement party is a celebratory gathering held after a couple gets engaged and before any other pre-wedding events. Think of it as the official kickoff to the wedding planning journey: a chance to share your news, introduce families from both sides, and enjoy the excitement before the logistics of seating charts and vendor contracts take over. It is not a bridal shower, a rehearsal dinner, or a bachelor or bachelorette party. Those come later. The engagement party sits at the very beginning of the pre-wedding event timeline, ideally two to four months after the proposal. It is the only celebration where both sides of the guest list come together before the wedding day itself. Traditionally, the bride’s parents hosted the engagement party. Today, either set of parents, a sibling, a close friend, or the couple themselves can take on the role. The party is also entirely optional. Some couples skip it, and that is perfectly fine. But if you do decide to celebrate, having a clear plan makes all the difference. One timing note worth keeping in mind: December is the peak proposal month, accounting for up to 16 percent of annual engagements. That makes January through March the busiest window for engagement party planning. If you got engaged during the holiday season, you are in good company. Engagement Party Etiquette: Rules Every Host and Guest Should Know Etiquette questions are the number one source of engagement party stress. These eight rules cover the situations that come up most often, from guest list politics to gift expectations. Anyone invited to the engagement party must be invited to the wedding. This is the most universally agreed-upon rule across all major wedding publications. If your wedding guest list is not finalized, keep the engagement party small: closest friends and immediate family only. Inviting someone to the party and then not following up with a wedding invitation creates genuine hurt feelings. The host pays for everything. Whoever organizes the party covers venue, food, drinks, and decorations. Guests should never be asked to contribute financially or pay for their own meals. If the budget is tight, scale the party format down rather than passing costs to attendees. Anyone can host. While parents traditionally took the lead, siblings, friends, or the couple themselves are all perfectly appropriate hosts in 2026. There are no gatekeepers here. The only guideline is that whoever hosts should genuinely want to do it, not feel pressured into the role. Schedule the party before any other pre-wedding events. The engagement party should come first on the celebration timeline, ahead of bridal showers, bachelor or bachelorette parties, and the rehearsal dinner. It should also not fall within two months of the wedding date, when everyone’s focus will be on the big day. Avoid scheduling your party on or adjacent to major holidays like Thanksgiving, Christmas, New Year’s Eve, or Valentine’s Day, when guests already have competing plans. Gifts are appreciated but never expected or solicited. Many guests bring something small (wine, a candle, a card), but there is no obligation. A simple “your presence is enough” on the invitation or wedding website sets the right tone. Registry information belongs on your wedding website, not the invitation. If guests ask where you are registered, point them to your wedding website where they can find your wish list on their own terms. Putting registry details on the invitation feels like a gift request, which is the opposite of the message you want to send. Multiple engagement parties are acceptable. If both sets of parents want to host, or you have friend groups in different cities, separate parties with different hosts and guest lists are completely fine. Each party can have its own format and vibe. Match the dress code to the venue and format. A backyard BBQ calls for casual attire. A private dining room calls for cocktail dress. Specify the dress code on the invitation so guests do not have to guess or stress about what to wear. Pro tip: The single most common engagement party mistake is inviting someone who will not make the wedding guest list. Before you finalize your party list, compare it against your working wedding list. If a name appears on the party list but not the wedding list, remove it now to avoid an awkward situation later. How to Plan an Engagement Party Step by Step Use this eight-week countdown checklist to stay on track. Each milestone builds on the last, so start at the top and work your way down. If you have less than eight weeks, compress the first two milestones into one week and prioritize venue, guest list, and invitations. 8-Week Engagement Party Planning Checklist Timeline Tasks 8 weeks before Choose a host and set a budget. Decide on the party format (cocktail, brunch, dinner, BBQ). Start drafting the guest list and cross-referencing it with your working wedding list. 6 to 7 weeks before Book your venue or confirm at-home logistics (tables, chairs, parking). Create a free wedding website to share event details, directions, and eventually your registry. Learn how to set up your site in minutes . 5 to 6 weeks before Send invitations (paper or digital). Include an RSVP deadline set for two weeks before the event. Use a tool to track responses digitally and collect dietary restrictions along with plus-one confirmations. 4 weeks before Finalize the menu and drinks. Book a caterer or plan your DIY menu. Order decorations. Start your registry so guests who ask about gifts can find your wish list on your website. 3 weeks before Plan games and activities. Create a playlist (aim for at least three hours of music). Arrange a photographer if desired. 2 weeks before RSVP deadline arrives. Confirm the final headcount with your venue or caterer. Finalize seating arrangements or the flow of the event space. 1 week before Confirm all vendors and delivery times. Prepare a rain plan or indoor backup. Assign day-of duties to helpers (setup, greeting, bar, cleanup). Day of Arrive two to three hours early for setup. Brief helpers on their roles. Take a deep breath and enjoy the celebration. Couples who build their wedding website early tend to stay ahead on every milestone that follows. According to Joy platform data, couples who launch their site before the engagement party complete 30 percent more planning tasks in the first three months compared to those who wait until closer to the wedding date. Engagement Party Budget Breakdown Budget is the area where most planning guides fall short, offering vague advice like “set a budget that works for you” without providing actual numbers. Here are real cost ranges to work with, broken down by party format and per-guest spending. Cost by Party Format Format Guest Count Estimated Cost Per-Guest Cost At-home or backyard 15 to 30 $300 to $1,500 $15 to $50 Restaurant private room 20 to 50 $1,000 to $4,000 $40 to $80 Bar, brewery, or winery 20 to 40 $800 to $3,000 $30 to $75 Catered event venue 50 to 100 $2,500 to $8,000 $50 to $100 Per-Guest Food and Drink Math Light refreshments (appetizers plus beer and wine): $15 to $25 per guest Full-service catering with open bar: $40 to $100 per guest Bite count rule: Plan six to eight bites per guest for a two-hour cocktail party Variety rule: Budget four to six hors d’oeuvres varieties for groups under 30 Budget-Saving Tips Host at home to eliminate venue fees entirely Choose brunch over evening cocktails (lower alcohol costs, shorter event duration) Ask a talented friend to handle photography instead of hiring a professional Set up a DIY signature cocktail station instead of a full open bar Use digital invitations to save $100 or more on paper and postage Borrow or rent serving platters, glassware, and linens instead of buying Choose reusable or compostable tableware to reduce waste and save on disposable supplies Add a cash fund to your registry for honeymoon or experience contributions as an alternative to physical gifts Choosing the Right Venue for Your Engagement Party The venue sets the tone for everything else: food, dress code, decorations, and overall vibe. A backyard party naturally leads to casual attire and a BBQ menu, while a private dining room steers you toward cocktail dress and a plated dinner. Use this comparison to match your party vision with the right space. Venue Type Best For Capacity Formality Avg. Cost At-home or backyard Intimate groups, budget-conscious hosts 15 to 40 Casual $300 to $1,500 Restaurant private room Couples who want a curated menu without the planning 20 to 50 Semi-formal $1,000 to $4,000 Bar, brewery, or winery Social, relaxed atmosphere with built-in drinks 20 to 40 Casual $800 to $3,000 Rooftop or garden Warm-weather celebrations with scenic backdrops 30 to 80 Semi-formal to formal $1,500 to $5,000 Event venue (loft, gallery) Themed or larger parties with full creative control 50 to 100+ Any $2,500 to $8,000 For couples with geographically scattered families, a destination engagement party can bring everyone together in a neutral location. Keep in mind that travel costs add up for guests, so provide plenty of advance notice (eight weeks minimum) and consider group hotel rates to ease the expense. If some loved ones cannot attend in person, consider a virtual or hybrid option. Set up a livestream through a laptop or tablet at the venue so long-distance family members and friends can watch toasts, play along with games, and feel included in the celebration. A dedicated video link shared through your wedding website keeps everyone connected without requiring complicated technology. Venue Booking Checklist Before signing a contract, confirm these details with any venue: Maximum capacity (seated vs. standing) Catering policy (in-house only, or outside vendors allowed) Rain plan or indoor backup space Parking availability and public transit access Wheelchair accessibility, elevator access, and restroom accessibility Noise restrictions and curfew times Minimum spend requirements (common at restaurants and bars) Engagement Party Themes and Ideas for 2026 The best engagement party themes feel like the couple, not like something pulled from a generic Pinterest board. Here are ideas organized by season, style, and activity to help spark your vision. By Season Spring: Garden brunch with fresh florals, pastel linens, and a mimosa bar. Think peonies on every table and croissants piled high. Summer: Backyard BBQ or pool party with lawn games, cold drinks, and a self-serve ice cream station for dessert. Fall: Harvest dinner with candles, pumpkins, warm cider cocktails, and a long communal table under the trees. Winter: Cozy cocktail party with a fireplace, hot cocoa bar, string lights, and rich jewel-tone decor. By Style Elegant: Black-tie dinner at a private dining room with plated courses, champagne, and a live jazz trio Casual: Taco bar and margaritas in the backyard with lawn games and a speaker playing your favorite playlist Boho: Picnic-style gathering on blankets with macrame accents, dried flowers, and a charcuterie spread Modern minimalist: Loft party with clean lines, a single signature cocktail, and a curated playlist that doubles as a conversation starter Activity-Based Ideas Cooking class for 10 to 20 guests at a local culinary studio Wine or cocktail tasting at a vineyard with a guided tour Bowling alley takeover with custom lane signs and a pizza buffet Brunch followed by a boat cruise or sunset sail Outdoor movie night with a projector, blankets, and popcorn bar For more inspiration, explore 40 or more engagement party themes and activities to find the right fit for your celebration. Pro tip: Pick a theme that reflects you as a couple, not what you think an engagement party “should” look like. The best parties feel authentic. If you bonded over tacos, throw a taco party. If you love craft beer, book a brewery. Your guests will remember the personality, not the perfection. Food, Drinks, and Menu Planning Food and drinks typically make up 50 to 70 percent of your engagement party budget. Getting the quantities right prevents both waste and the dreaded empty platter at hour two. Below are formulas, per-guest calculations, and menu suggestions organized by party format. How Much Food to Plan Two-hour cocktail party: Six to eight bites per guest, four to six hors d’oeuvres varieties. Focus on a mix of hot and cold options. Three-hour dinner party: Appetizer course, main course, and dessert. Budget $40 to $80 per guest depending on the service style. Brunch: Waffle or pancake station, fruit, pastries, and one egg dish. Budget $20 to $40 per guest. Brunch tends to be the most budget-friendly format. Drink Planning Beer and wine only: Budget two to three drinks per guest for the first hour, then one drink per guest for each additional hour Signature cocktail: Choose one drink that represents you as a couple and display the recipe on a sign near the bar. This adds personality and simplifies bartending. Non-alcoholic options: Always provide at least two (sparkling water and a mocktail, flavored lemonade, or iced tea). About 30 percent of guests will appreciate a non-alcoholic alternative. Menu Ideas by Format Format Menu Style Example Items Cocktail party Passed hors d’oeuvres and stations Bruschetta, shrimp skewers, cheese board, crudites Sit-down dinner Plated or family-style Salad, protein entree, seasonal sides, dessert BBQ or cookout Buffet-style Sliders, grilled chicken, corn, coleslaw, watermelon Brunch Stations and self-serve Waffle bar, fruit display, quiche, mimosa station Always ask guests about dietary restrictions when they RSVP. Even a small party of 25 will likely include at least one or two guests with allergies, vegetarian preferences, or other dietary needs. Collecting this information early gives you time to plan alternatives. Engagement Party Invitations: Timing and Wording Examples Send your engagement party invitations four to six weeks before the event. Set the RSVP deadline for two weeks before the party so you have time to confirm the headcount with your venue or caterer and make any last-minute adjustments. Digital invitations are perfectly appropriate for casual and semi-formal parties, and they have the added benefit of built-in RSVP tracking. For formal events, paper invitations add a polished touch. Regardless of format, never include registry information on the invitation itself. Sample Invitation Wording Casual: “Join us for drinks and appetizers as we celebrate [Name] and [Name]’s engagement! Saturday, [Date] at 6 PM. [Venue/Address]. RSVP by [Date].” Semi-formal: “[Host Name(s)] invite you to an engagement party honoring [Name] and [Name]. [Date] at [Time]. [Venue]. Dinner and cocktails. Please respond by [Date].” Formal: “[Host Name(s)] request the pleasure of your company at a dinner celebrating the engagement of [Name] and [Name]. [Date, Time, Venue]. Kindly respond by [Date].” After sending invitations, track responses with a digital tool that collects headcounts, dietary restrictions, plus-one confirmations, and mailing addresses you will need for wedding invitations later. Look for a platform that lets guests RSVP with meal preferences and address details in a single step, so you are not chasing replies across email, text, and social media. Having this information in one place saves hours of follow-up and keeps your guest data organized as you transition into wedding planning. Day-of Timeline, Decorations, and Activities You have planned for weeks. Now it is time to execute. This day-of timeline keeps things running smoothly without making you feel like an event coordinator instead of the guest of honor. Day-of Setup Timeline Time Task 3 hours before Arrive at venue. Set up tables, signage, and the welcome area. 2 hours before Arrange florals, candles, and photo backdrop. Set up bar and food stations. 1 hour before Final walk-through of the space. Brief helpers on their duties. Cue the playlist. Guests arrive Host greets at the door. Drinks begin flowing. Let conversation build naturally. 1 hour in Games or activities begin. Toast from the host or parents. 2 hours in Dessert or engagement cake. Informal mingling. Photo booth opens. 3 to 4 hours in Wind down. Distribute favors if planned. Thank guests personally as they leave. Engagement Party Favor Ideas Party favors are optional but add a thoughtful finishing touch. Keep them simple, useful, and aligned with your party theme. Custom cookies or macarons: $2 to $4 per guest. Order them in your wedding colors or with your initials. Mini candles or matchboxes: $1 to $3 per guest. Choose a scent that matches the season. Small succulents or seed packets: $2 to $5 per guest. A living keepsake guests can take home and grow. Miniature bottles of olive oil, honey, or hot sauce: $3 to $6 per guest. Pair with a custom label featuring the couple’s names and engagement date. Decorations That Set the Tone Use the three-element rule: pick three decor categories and skip the rest to avoid clutter. Your engagement party does not need to rival the wedding in scale or expense. Must-haves: Welcome sign with the couple’s names, one consistent centerpiece style (florals or candles), and ambient lighting (candles or string lights) Nice-to-haves: Photo backdrop or polaroid wall, dessert table styling, custom napkins or stirrers Skip for now: Elaborate floral arches, chair covers, or large balloon installations. Save the major decor investment for the wedding day. Games and Activities Guests Will Love Games work best when they are easy to explain, quick to play, and do not put introverted guests on the spot. Here are five crowd-tested options. He Said / She Said: Guests guess which partner said a given quote or answer. Print cards in advance and provide pens at each table. Engagement bingo: Hand out bingo cards filled with wedding-related prompts (someone cries, someone asks about the ring, the couple kisses). First to complete a row wins a small prize. Advice cards: Set out cards and pens so guests can write marriage advice for the couple. These double as a meaningful keepsake you will revisit for years. Photo booth or polaroid station: Provide fun props (hats, signs, oversized glasses) and a guest book where guests paste their photos alongside a personal note. Cocktail-naming contest: Guests invent and name the couple’s signature wedding drink. The winning recipe makes it to the reception bar menu. What to Wear to an Engagement Party When in doubt, take your cue from the venue and the invitation. Here is a quick guide by formality level. Casual (backyard, BBQ, brunch): Sundresses, chinos and a button-down, smart sandals or clean sneakers Semi-formal (restaurant, rooftop): Cocktail dress or jumpsuit, blazer and slacks, heels or loafers Formal (private dining, black-tie dinner): Floor-length gown or tailored suit, statement jewelry, dress shoes The engaged person can absolutely wear white. It is their celebration and a great opportunity to embrace the moment. Guests, however, should avoid white unless the invitation explicitly says otherwise. If you are unsure about the dress code, check the invitation for cues or ask the host directly. Most guests prefer to be slightly overdressed than underdressed, so when in doubt, go one level up. After the Party: Follow-Up and Next Steps The celebration does not end when the last guest leaves. A few follow-up tasks in the days after the party set a gracious tone and help you carry momentum into wedding planning. Send thank-you notes within two weeks. A brief handwritten note to each guest (and especially to anyone who brought a gift) goes a long way. Mention something specific about their presence or gift to make it personal. Share photos through your wedding website. Upload a curated gallery so guests can revisit the evening and download their favorites. This also gives long-distance loved ones a chance to see what they missed. Transition your guest list into wedding planning. Use the RSVP data and mailing addresses you collected to start building your wedding guest list and save-the-date mailing list. Respect photo-sharing boundaries. Before posting engagement party photos on social media, check with the couple (if you are a guest) or with guests (if you are the couple) about tagging preferences and timing. Not everyone wants to appear on social media without advance notice. Frequently Asked Questions About Engagement Parties Who hosts and pays for an engagement party? Traditionally the bride’s parents hosted and paid, but today it can be either set of parents, both sets jointly, the couple themselves, or a close friend or sibling. Whoever hosts the party is responsible for covering the costs, including venue, food, drinks, and decorations. Guests should never be asked to pay for their own meals or drinks at an engagement party. How soon after getting engaged should you have an engagement party? Plan your engagement party for two to four months after the proposal, while the excitement is still fresh and before wedding planning stress sets in. The party should take place before any other pre-wedding events like bridal showers or bachelor parties, and should not be scheduled within two months of the wedding date. How much does an engagement party cost in 2026? Most engagement parties cost between $1,000 and $5,000. An at-home party for 15 to 30 guests typically runs $300 to $1,500 with no venue fee. A restaurant private room for 20 to 50 guests costs $1,000 to $4,000, usually as a food-and-beverage minimum. A catered venue party for 50 to 100 guests runs $2,500 to $8,000 including catering, rentals, and staff. Do guests bring gifts to an engagement party? Gifts are not expected at an engagement party, though many guests bring something small like wine, a candle, or a card. Registry information should never appear on the engagement party invitation. Instead, share your registry link on your wedding website for guests who ask. Always acknowledge any gift received with a prompt handwritten thank-you note. Should everyone invited to the engagement party also be invited to the wedding? Yes. This is the most universally agreed-upon engagement party etiquette rule. Anyone who receives an engagement party invitation expects to also be invited to the wedding. If your wedding guest list is not finalized, keep the engagement party smaller with only your closest friends and immediate family to avoid commitments you cannot keep.

body_text: View All News Savara Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Provides Business Update August 11, 2026 Download (opens in new window) MOLBREEVI* BLA PDUFA Target Action Date Set for November 22, 2026 MOLBREEVI MAAs Under Review by the EMA and the U.K.’s MHRA; Decisions Expected in Q1 2027 and Q4 2026, respectively Data Presented at ATS Showed Molgramostim Demonstrated Continuous Long-term Improvements in Lung Function and Respiratory Health-Related Quality of Life European and Australian Patent Offices Granted MOLBREEVI Liquid Formulation Patents, Providing Protection until March 2041 ~$173M in Cash and Short-Term Investments as of June 30, 2026, Plus up to ~$150M of Non-Dilutive Capital Upon FDA Approval of MOLBREEVI, Positions the Company Well for Launch LANGHORNE, Pa.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Savara Inc. (Nasdaq: SVRA) (the Company), a clinical stage biopharmaceutical company focused on rare respiratory diseases, reported financial results for the second quarter ending June 30, 2026 and provided a business update. “While we have regulatory applications under review across the U.S., EU, and U.K., the U.S. represents our nearest-term opportunity,” said Matt Pauls, J.D., M.B.A., Chair and Chief Executive Officer, Savara. “Our focus is on the potential launch of MOLBREEVI in the U.S., supported by a strong balance sheet to ensure commercial readiness.” Second Quarter Financial Results (Unaudited) Savara's net loss for the second quarter of 2026 was $40.2 million, or $(0.16) per share of which $7.8 million was related to non-cash share-based compensation expense compared with a net loss of $30.4 million, or $(0.14) per share of which $2.7 million was related to share-based compensation expense, for the second quarter of 2025. Research and development expenses increased by $1.2 million, or 5.8%, to $22.0 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026 from $20.8 million for the three months ended June 30, 2025. This increase was primarily due to $2.0 million of higher personnel costs, mainly related to increased stock-based compensation expense, partially offset by the performance of tasks related to our MOLBREEVI program, which included a decrease of $0.2 million of costs related to our chemistry, manufacturing, and controls activities, primarily driven by activity at our drug substance manufacturer, and a decrease of $0.6 million of costs related to regulatory affairs and quality assurance consulting. General and administrative expenses increased by $8.3 million, or 78.2%, to $19.0 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026 from $10.7 million for the three months ended June 30, 2025. The increase was primarily attributable to $7.5 million higher personnel costs, driven by increased stock-based compensation expense as well as increased headcount as we build out our commercial team in support of our planned product launch, in addition to an increase of $0.8 million in certain commercial activities. These investments reflect our strategy to establish the commercial infrastructure necessary to support an effective and timely launch. As of June 30, 2026, the Company had cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments of ~$173.0 million and debt of ~$30.1 million. About Autoimmune Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis (Autoimmune PAP) Autoimmune PAP is a rare lung disease characterized by the abnormal build-up of surfactant in the alveoli. Surfactant consists of proteins and lipids and is an important physiological substance that lines the alveoli to prevent them from collapsing. In a healthy lung, excess surfactant is cleared and digested by immune cells called alveolar macrophages. Alveolar macrophages need to be stimulated by granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) to function properly in clearing surfactant, but in autoimmune PAP, GM-CSF is neutralized by autoantibodies against GM-CSF, rendering macrophages unable to adequately clear surfactant. As a result, an excess of surfactant accumulates in the alveoli, causing impaired gas transfer, resulting in clinical symptoms of shortness of breath, often with cough and frequent fatigue. Patients may also experience episodes of fever, chest pain, or coughing up blood, especially if secondary lung infection develops. In the long term, the disease can lead to serious complications, including lung fibrosis and the need for a lung transplant. About Savara Savara is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on rare respiratory diseases. Our lead program, MOLBREEVI*, is a recombinant human granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) in Phase 3 development for autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (autoimmune PAP). MOLBREEVI is delivered via an investigational eFlow® Nebulizer System (PARI Pharma GmbH) specifically developed for inhalation of a large molecule. Our management team has significant experience in rare respiratory diseases and pulmonary medicine, identifying unmet needs, and effectively advancing product candidates to approval and commercialization. More information can be found at www.savarapharma.com and LinkedIn . *MOLBREEVI is the proposed trade name for molgramostim inhalation solution. It is not approved in any indication.
